shape_target: 600-1200 chars per text, multi-sentence paragraphs at production-ingest shape
notes: V3 production-shape rewrite of V2 SCR prototypes. The V2 prototypes were sentence-level (median 74 chars) and produced macro-F1 0.929 in-distribution but 100% under-threshold on LoCoMo per-session (median 2808 chars) and 93% on LME per-turn (median 482 chars). V3 keeps the V2 4-role taxonomy (state_change_report, investigation, observation, preference) and the V2 style guide constraints, but expands each prototype to a production-shape paragraph that reads like an actual chat/dialogue/session blob.

state_change_report.text: OTLP migration completed at the platform level. Production logging pipelines have been running on OTLP exclusively since the 2026-03-12 release window. The legacy JSON ingest path was decommissioned that same week, and the Splunk forwarders that fed the prior pipeline were retired. Internal dashboards confirm OTLP traces are flowing at the expected volume, and the OpenTelemetry collector fleet now handles roughly 3.2M spans per minute at peak. Engineering has stopped issuing legacy log API tokens; the existing tokens will expire on rotation. The storage backend was pruned of pre-OTLP indexes, and retention policies were updated to a 30-day hot, 180-day cold tier. The pre-cutover OTLP ingestion validation runbook has been archived to the SRE knowledge base.

The internal Grafana stack went live on 2026-02-08 and Datadog dashboards were decommissioned that week. Every team-owned dashboard has been migrated, and access is now scoped through SSO with role-based permissions configured for SRE, platform, and product orgs. The Datadog org was placed in read-only mode on 2026-02-15 and fully closed on 2026-03-01 after the export of historical metrics completed. Grafana Tempo has been receiving traces since 2026-02-20, replacing the prior trace tier. Internal alerting channels have been redirected from the Datadog monitor outputs to Grafana Alertmanager. The migration runbook, the dashboards-as-code repository, and the post-migration validation report have all been published to the platform-docs space, and the executive dashboard owners have signed off on the new layout.

Bazel has been the polyglot monorepo build system since 2026-01-30 and the previous Make scripts were archived. All 14 services in the monorepo have working Bazel build targets, and CI has been driving builds and tests through Bazel for every PR since the cutover. Remote caching went live on 2026-02-05 and the average cold-build time on CI dropped from 18 minutes to 4.5 minutes; the remote-cache hit rate has held above 88% for three consecutive weeks. The legacy Make scripts were preserved at /docs/legacy/Makefiles for reference but are not invoked anywhere in CI or local dev. The Bazel toolchain version is pinned in the workspace and bumped through a controlled monthly release.

The 1-approver typo-fix policy has been in effect since 2026-02-14 and applies to PRs that only modify markdown, comments, or string literals matched by the typo-only ruleset. The rule was implemented in the Conductor branch protection layer, and the PR template now exposes a check-box that clearly distinguishes typo-only from substantive changes. Auto-merge for dependabot-only PRs went live on 2026-03-01 with required passing CI as the sole gate. The metrics dashboard has tracked PR-to-merge time since the change; the median for typo-only PRs dropped from 1.6 days to under 4 hours, and dependabot PRs from 3 days to about 2 hours. The policies have been documented in the platform handbook since 2026-02-10, and the rollout runbook was archived to the engineering-ops space.

Daily oncall handoffs replaced the weekly rotation on 2026-03-15. Each shift is now 24 hours, with a 30-minute structured handoff at 09:00 PT and a backup at 17:00 PT. The PagerDuty schedule was updated that same week, and team leads adjusted on-call compensation accordingly. PagerDuty has been the oncall platform since 2026-02-01 after Opsgenie was sunsetted that month; the Opsgenie integrations were removed from internal services in two batches across early February. Daily handoff templates have been published in the oncall handbook, and the 2026-03-22 retro confirmed adoption across all 6 platform teams. The pager-fatigue metric measured on the new cadence has held at 22% lower than the weekly-rotation baseline for the past three weeks.

investigation.text: We are investigating why the log ingestion pipeline drops roughly 4% of records during peak hours. The drops cluster between 11:30 and 14:00 PT on weekdays, which lines up with our highest-traffic window but not perfectly with the deploy schedule. The current working theory is that the OTLP receivers are being throttled by the upstream load balancer, but we have not been able to confirm yet because the LB's metrics surface is sparse during the affected windows. The team is running tcpdump captures on three of the receiver pods today, and we added structured-context fields to the dropped-record events so we can correlate them with downstream timeouts. We expect the captures to land tomorrow and the pattern should be visible in the analysis. No customer-facing signal has been impacted; the dropped events are duplicated in the resilience tier and replay successfully on a 5-minute lag, but we still want to root-cause the throttle behavior before the next deploy.

Looking into why the Grafana home dashboard loads slowly for new users on first sign-in. The complaint surfaced from three product teams in the past week, and a fourth team reported it during the 2026-04-21 sync. We have not been able to reproduce the slowness on existing accounts, which makes the diagnosis tricky. Initial profiling shows that the org-discovery query on the new-user code path issues five sequential calls to the auth service, and we suspect that pattern is the root cause but we need to verify against logs. The team is enabling RUM capture for the home dashboard route this week, and we have a tracing PR up to add spans across the auth fan-out. We expect the data by next Monday. No production rollout depends on this, but the new-user onboarding metric has trended down 8% since the new home dashboard rolled out, so we want a real answer before quarter close.

Root-causing why CI builds intermittently fail at the dependency-fetch step on the polyglot monorepo. The pattern has been showing up about once every 30 builds for the past two weeks, and it is not concentrated on any single language toolchain. We have ruled out the obvious upstream-registry outage hypothesis because the failures persist when we point Bazel at our internal mirror. We are exploring whether the remote cache is partially returning corrupted artifacts, which would match the observed retry-success behavior. The team has instrumented the Bazel fetch step with finer-grained timing and added a checksum log on every cache hit. We expect to have data within a few CI cycles. We are also evaluating whether to set a lower retry threshold so we get faster signal during CI failures, but no decision has been made yet because the cost of premature retries is non-trivial on the queue.

Trying to understand why bot-flagged PRs sit in review for an average of 5 or more days even when CI is green and the changes are small. The pattern was first surfaced by the engineering productivity team in the 2026-04-15 review, and we have been digging since. We are looking at three angles: are reviewers de-prioritizing bot-flagged PRs because they assume the bots are noisy; is the notification routing for bot-flagged PRs failing to land in the right Slack channels; and is there a queueing effect where bot-flagged PRs accumulate on a small set of approvers. We have not been able to confirm any of these yet because the GitHub timeline data does not directly show reviewer attention. The team is wiring up a custom event stream from the GitHub webhooks and expects to have a usable signal by next sprint. No remediation has been chosen yet.

Diagnosing the pager-fatigue trend showing up in the recent oncall surveys. The 2026-04-10 quarterly survey reported a 12-point increase in fatigue scores across the platform org, and the open-text responses pointed at three potential contributors: increased page volume from a recent service launch, lower-quality runbooks for the affected services, and a perceived weakening of the daily-handoff handoff template. We are running structured 1:1 conversations with the most-affected oncall engineers this week, and we are pulling the page-volume timeseries to see whether the increase is statistically meaningful or noise from the new service. The team has not committed to any remediation; we want to confirm which of the three contributors is dominant before we change the oncall rotation or invest in runbook improvements.

observation.text: Logs from the past two weeks show a consistent pattern in error rates across the edge proxies. Roughly 12% of error events are being silently dropped at the egress layer before they reach the central pipeline. The drop rate correlates strongly with the deploy times of the proxy fleet's traffic-shaping module, with a 30-minute lag after each rollout. Volume measurements indicate the affected proxies are processing about 2.1 million requests per hour during the dropped windows, and the lost events appear to be concentrated in the 502 and 504 status codes. Records show the issue began on 2026-04-09, two weeks after the new traffic-shaping code shipped, and the rate has been stable since then. The dashboard that tracks this metric has been updated to highlight the discrepancy with a yellow band, and the SRE on-call has been adding the data point to the daily handoff notes.

Grafana dashboard load metrics show p95 render time on the home dashboard rose from 280ms to 410ms over the past three weeks. The p99 figure rose more sharply, from 480ms to 920ms, and the long tail correlates with the introduction of the new tenant-aware widgets. Volume is steady at about 14,000 dashboard loads per hour at business peak, with no notable change in user count. The Tempo tracing data captures 2.4M spans per minute on the affected route, of which roughly 8% exceed the 500ms SLO budget. We see the same regression on the team-overview dashboard but not on the per-service drill-down, which suggests the cost is concentrated in the aggregate widgets. The metrics have been visible in the platform health board since 2026-04-12, and the post-mortem channel has been quiet on this thread.

Build logs from the last 30 days indicate the dependency cache hit rate dropped from 92% to 78% across the polyglot monorepo. The drop is concentrated in the JVM toolchain targets, where the rate fell to 64%; the Go and Python toolchains held steady at 89% and 91% respectively. CI queue measurements show post-lunch deploy windows back up to about 80 builds during peak, double the morning queue depth. The remote-cache size was measured at 412GB last week, up 18% from the prior month, and pruning policy logs indicate roughly 6% of artifacts are evicted under LRU each day. Build runtime distribution shows a long tail above 9 minutes for the affected JVM targets. The trends have been visible on the build-perf dashboard since 2026-04-08, and the data was discussed in the 2026-04-22 platform sync.

Code review metrics show the median time-to-review at 1.7 days, up from 1.1 days last month. The data is broken down by team and the increase concentrates on the platform and infra orgs, where the median climbed to 2.3 and 2.1 days respectively. Three PRs were merged this week without the required test coverage, all from the platform org, and the linter shows that none of them tripped the auto-skip rule for typo-only changes. The PR queue depth dashboard records 142 open PRs in the platform org as of 2026-04-26, the highest number recorded since instrumentation began. The number of self-merged PRs has held flat at 4% of total, but the share of dependabot auto-merges grew to 18% after the auto-merge policy went live. The metrics review committee flagged the trends on the 2026-04-25 staff sync.

Oncall dashboard data shows page volume up 22% week-over-week across the platform org. The increase concentrates on the data-platform service group, which saw a 41% jump driven by the new ingestion job rolling out in production. The oncall response p95 is now 8 minutes versus last quarter's 4 minutes; the regression is concentrated on weekend shifts where the secondary oncall coverage is thinnest. Survey results indicate 30% of oncall engineers reported skipping the new handoff template in the most recent week, citing time pressure from the increased page volume. PagerDuty escalation logs show a 14% rise in escalations to secondary oncall in the past two weeks, and the data is consistent across the three platform teams. The metrics have been live on the oncall-health dashboard since the daily-handoff cutover.

preference.text: Personally I lean toward making OTLP the only logging path going forward, even for the legacy services that still emit JSON. The team has discussed this in three different review cycles, and my position has been consistent: maintaining two pipelines doubles the operational surface for marginal gain on the legacy side. I would rather see us invest the cycles freed up by the migration in better trace sampling and more useful structured-context fields than keep dual-format support. My preference is to retire JSON ingest entirely by Q3, with a clear deprecation notice to internal teams. Recommend we set the deprecation review for the next platform sync. I would also argue we don't need to gate this on the smaller services completing their own migrations, since we can build a translation layer at the edge if needed. None of this is committed yet; we should have the broader conversation first, but my stance is clear.

The team's preference is to converge on a single canonical home dashboard rather than maintain three role-specific variants. Personally I would rather have a smaller, more opinionated dashboard than a wide, configurable one that no role uses well. Recommend Grafana over Kibana for the dashboards-as-code workflow, mostly because the integration with our alerting layer is already wired up and the training cost is lower. My take is that the SRE oncall view should be the primary source of truth, and the executive view should pull from it via embedded widgets rather than from independent queries. Lean toward investing in dashboard-as-code tooling first, before we author another bespoke layout. I would advocate for a quarterly review cycle on dashboard ownership, but this is a soft preference; happy to defer to the platform team if they have a stronger position.

Prefer Bazel hermeticity over Make convenience for the polyglot stack, even at the cost of the steeper learning curve for new contributors. The team's preference, based on the 2026-Q1 retro, is to keep investing in remote caching rather than buying more CI hardware. My take is that we should set a hard rule for new services: Bazel-native targets only, no Makefile escape hatches. Recommend we publish a small starter template that gets new contributors productive in a day. Lean toward buying remote-cache capacity as a managed service rather than running our own; the cost difference is small and the operational burden is real. I would also rather invest in build-perf instrumentation than another retry knob in CI. None of this is decided; we should have the conversation at the next platform-perf review.

My preference is to keep 2-approver reviews on auth-touching code even at the velocity cost. Personally I would lean async over synchronous pair-review for non-urgent PRs, mostly because the synchronous mode burns reviewer attention disproportionately. The team's standing position is that bot-flagged PRs should not skip the human review gate even when CI is green. Recommend we leave the typo-fix 1-approver rule alone; the data so far supports keeping it. I would advocate for adding a new rule that auto-merges trivial documentation PRs when only the author is involved, but I am happy to defer if the platform team would rather hold the line. Lean toward writing more explicit reviewer-assignment heuristics rather than letting the round-robin allocator pick. None of this is committed; the policy review group meets next month.

In favor of moving to a follow-the-sun oncall structure once we have enough EU coverage to staff a second timezone reliably. My preference is to keep primary plus secondary oncall structure even after the team grows; the second pair of eyes during incidents has been valuable. Recommend we keep the daily-handoff cadence even though weekly rotations are operationally simpler. I would lean toward investing in better runbooks before we tweak rotation length further; the survey data points more strongly at runbook quality than at cadence. My take is that we should explicitly carve out a non-oncall focus week per engineer per quarter rather than expecting individuals to push back on rotation requests. None of this is decided; the oncall review committee meets in two weeks and we will have the broader conversation then.
